BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

Hans Peter Lyngsøe Raaschou-jensen Affiliation: University of Copenhagen    M. Onurcan Kaya Affiliation: Technical University of Denmark    Desmond Elliott Affiliation: University of Copenhagen
Abstract

Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.

1 Introduction

Parallel test-time scaling has become a practical way to spend more computation at inference time. The common recipe is to sample several candidate reasoning traces, then choose among them with voting, reranking, or verification (Wang et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2024; Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023). This can improve answer coverage, but the parallel traces in one rollout cannot reuse information from another. For example, if different traces explore different proof strategies, an intermediate lemma found in one trace is unavailable to the others until final aggregation. Parallel scaling therefore increases the number of computations, but it does not make those computations collaborative.

Final aggregation and verification can compare completed traces, but they do not let one stream change another stream’s computation during inference. This work asks whether sequence models can occupy a tunable middle ground between parallel and sequential scaling: keeping the diversity of parallel streams while allowing intentional communication during the forward pass. We introduce batch-mixing as a class of sequence models in which streams can attend to selected hidden states from their peers. Our concrete instantiation, BatchParScale, restricts this exchange to a small set of communication positions, so most tokens remain ordinary per-stream causal computation.

We evaluate this idea from several angles. Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack tests whether a stream without local evidence can recover information from another stream. TinyStories pretraining and FineWeb-Edu LoRA continued pretraining test whether the mechanism improves ordinary language-model objectives and masked-token recovery. Parallel QA-style probes test whether those gains correspond to reliable transfer of specific facts across streams. Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning tests whether the same communication primitive can support learned coordination. Finally, because sparse attention patterns can be asymptotically attractive but slow in practice, we analyze the direct implementation and an efficient two-pass version of BatchParScale.

BatchParScale can learn controlled cross-stream retrieval, improves aggregate language-model loss in our small-scale comparisons, and improves masked-token recovery when neighboring streams contain redundant context. LoRA continued pretraining shows that the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer, and MARL results show competitive performance on several coordination-sensitive tasks. However, aggregate loss improvements and masked-token recovery do not imply reliable transfer of specific facts to streams without local evidence. This failure mode is clearest in PNIAH and PMHQA, where for both pretrained and finetuned models performance remains close to random despite the model being able to solve the task perfectly when information remains in a single stream. On the other hand, performance on parallel-WikiHop remains meaningfully above random. This motivates treating better data augmentation and training objectives as open problems for future research.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate batch-mixingas a sequence-modeling primitive for communication between parallel streams, and instantiate it as BatchParScale.

  • •

    We introduce Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack (PNIAH) and parallel QA/MHQA (PQA/PMHQA)-style benchmarks for measuring whether information reaches streams that do not contain the evidence locally.

  • •

    We evaluate BatchParScale across language-model pretraining, LoRA continued pretraining, PNIAH and PMHQA, and cooperative MARL, finding that our architecture outperforms ParScale on sequence modelling, but performs poorly on downstream PNIAH and PMHQA-style benchmarks.

  • •

    We produce an efficient two-pass implementation that makes BatchParScale communication hardware-friendly.

2 Related Work

2.1 Parallel Reasoning and Test-Time Scaling

Recent work treats inference-time computation as a scaling axis for language models. These scaling methods allocate additional computation to sampling, verification, or refinement, and have been shown in certain cases to improve performance more efficiently than increasing model size (Snell et al., 2024). The most common parallel form is to sample multiple independent candidate solutions and aggregate them. Self-consistency uses this idea for chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer (Wang et al., 2023). Large Language Monkeys studies this repeated-sampling regime at much larger scale, showing that solution coverage can improve over many samples, especially in domains with reliable automatic verification (Brown et al., 2024). However, these approaches leave the underlying computations independent: each rollout is generated without access to the intermediate states or discoveries of the others.

Multi-Sequence Verifiers address this limitation by jointly processing a set of candidate answers instead of scoring each candidate independently (Kim et al., 2026). They improve best-of-NN selection and early stopping through an auxiliary verifier, but the reasoning streams themselves still do not communicate while generating.

ParScale scales inference differently, by running parallel prefix-conditioned forward passes over the same sequence rather than sampling independent outputs (Chen et al., 2025). It duplicates the input across PP streams that share a Transformer backbone; each stream prepends fixed, input-independent learned prefix tokens that diversify hidden states across streams. Their outputs are combined only at a final dynamic aggregation step, and the streams do not interact during the forward pass.

2.2 Sparse and Latent Attention

The Transformer introduced self-attention as the core sequence-modeling primitive (Vaswani et al., 2017). Encoder-decoder attention, in which queries come from one sequence and keys and values come from another, provides an early form of cross-sequence information exchange (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017). Subsequent work has studied sparse and latent variants of these attention structures. Sparse Transformer, Longformer, and BigBird reduce the overhead of dense self-attention through local, strided, random, or global connectivity patterns (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020). Longformer furthermore designates selected positions as global-attention sites and gives them dedicated query, key, and value projections rather than reusing the ordinary token projections. Set Transformer and Perceiver-style architectures introduce learned latent slots or inducing points that mediate attention over large collections of inputs (Lee et al., 2019; Jaegle et al., 2021; Jaegle et al., 2022). Our communication positions play a similar inducing-point role, but they are embedded inside otherwise independent streams and are constrained by causal sequence order.

2.3 Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Multi-agent reinforcement learning studies settings in which multiple agents learn policies while interacting through a shared environment (Tan, 1993; Littman, 1994; Busoniu et al., 2008). A common paradigm is centralized training with decentralized execution, where agents may use global information during training but act from local observations at test time (Oliehoek et al., 2008; Lowe et al., 2017). MADDPG introduced an actor-critic approach for mixed cooperative-competitive environments and popularized the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) benchmarks (Lowe et al., 2017). MAPPO later showed that a carefully tuned PPO implementation is a strong and simple baseline for cooperative MARL tasks (Schulman et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022).

A related line of work learns differentiable communication channels between separate actors. CommNet lets agents condition on an average of other agents’ hidden states (Sukhbaatar and Fergus, 2016); IC3Net adds learned gates that control when agents communicate (Singh et al., 2019); and TarMAC uses attention to make communication targeted across senders and receivers (Das et al., 2019). These methods establish continuous hidden-state exchange as a trainable component of cooperative decision-making systems. Our MARL experiments place batch-mixing in this lineage by treating each agent’s history as a stream and restricting cross-agent reads to selected communication positions.

Recent work has also applied sequence models to MARL. Multi-Agent Transformer formulates cooperative MARL as sequence modeling over agents and actions (Wen et al., 2022). Sable further studies scalable sequence models for MARL, emphasizing performance, memory efficiency, and scalability (Mahjoub et al., 2025). JAX-based environment suites have also made large batched RL experiments easier to run: Jumanji provides scalable single-agent environments and baselines (Bonnet et al., 2024), while JaxMARL extends this style of infrastructure to multi-agent environments and algorithms (Rutherford et al., 2023). Brax provides the differentiable physics backend used by continuous-control multi-agent environments such as MABrax (Freeman et al., 2021).

3 Method

3.1 ParScale

The model architecture most similar to our approach is ParScale (Chen et al., 2025). Given an input sequence

x=(x1,…,xn),x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),

ParScale duplicates the sequence into P∈ℕP\in\mathbb{N} parallel streams. Each stream is processed by the same Transformer backbone fθf_{\theta}, but the streams are distinguished by learned prefix key-value caches. For stream p∈{1,…,P}p\in\{1,\ldots,P\} and layer ℓ\ell, let

Πp(ℓ)=(Kp,pre(ℓ),Vp,pre(ℓ))\Pi^{(\ell)}_{p}=\left(K^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}},V^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}}\right)

denote the stream-specific learned prefix cache, with prefix length q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}. For one attention head we have:

Kp,pre(ℓ),Vp,pre(ℓ)∈ℝq×dh.K^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}},V^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times d_{h}}.

If the ordinary hidden states in stream pp produce queries, keys, and values

Qp(ℓ),Kp,x(ℓ),Vp,x(ℓ)∈ℝn×dhQ^{(\ell)}_{p},\quad K^{(\ell)}_{p,x},\quad V^{(\ell)}_{p,x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}}

then the attention operation in ParScale is schematically

K~p(ℓ)=Concat⁡[Kp,pre(ℓ);Kp,x(ℓ)],\displaystyle\widetilde{K}^{(\ell)}_{p}=\operatorname{Concat}\left[K^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}};K^{(\ell)}_{p,x}\right],
V~p(ℓ)=Concat⁡[Vp,pre(ℓ);Vp,x(ℓ)],\displaystyle\widetilde{V}^{(\ell)}_{p}=\operatorname{Concat}\left[V^{(\ell)}_{p,\mathrm{pre}};V^{(\ell)}_{p,x}\right],
Attn⁡(Qp(ℓ),K~p(ℓ),V~p(ℓ)).\operatorname{Attn}\left(Q^{(\ell)}_{p},\,\widetilde{K}^{(\ell)}_{p},\,\widetilde{V}^{(\ell)}_{p}\right).

Thus, all streams receive the same token sequence xx, but stream pp attends with its own learned prefix cache at every layer. We can summarize the resulting model as

gθ​(x)=∑p=1Pwp​fθ​(xp),g_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{p=1}^{P}w_{p}f_{\theta}(x_{p}),

where xpx_{p} denotes the pp-th prefix-conditioned stream and wpw_{p} is its aggregation weight. The backbone parameters θ\theta are shared across all streams; only the prefix caches and aggregation parameters are stream-specific.

The aggregation weights are computed dynamically from the stream outputs, using an MLP

h:ℝdo×P→ℝPh:\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}\times P}\to\mathbb{R}^{P}

that maps stream outputs to PP logits.

The aggregation weights are computed as

𝐰=Softmax⁡(h⁡([fθ​(x1);…;fθ​(xP)])).\mathbf{w}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(h\left(\left[f_{\theta}(x_{1});\ldots;f_{\theta}(x_{P})\right]\right)\right).

Training optimizes standard next-token cross-entropy on the aggregated output of gθg_{\theta}, so all PP streams contribute to a single prediction at each position rather than receiving separate per-stream losses. To avoid collapse, label smoothing is also applied to the aggregation weights,

wp←wp​(1−ϵ)+ϵP,w_{p}\leftarrow w_{p}(1-\epsilon)+\frac{\epsilon}{P},

which acts as a load-balancing regularizer and prevents a few streams from dominating the mixture early in training.

ParScale increases computation by evaluating PP prefix-conditioned versions of the same sequence through a shared Transformer. The streams are diverse because they use different learned prefix key-value caches, but they remain independent while processing the sequence. Their only interaction occurs at the final dynamic aggregation step. The cost of adding sparse cross-stream communication is analyzed in Section 8.

3.2 Batch-Mixing

Transformer layers usually mix hidden states along two axes. Given hidden states X∈ℝB×S×DX\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times D}, the MLP block is a channel mixer: it applies the same token-wise map over the feature dimension,

Xb,t,:↦MLP(Xb,t,:),X_{b,t,:}\mapsto\operatorname{MLP}(X_{b,t,:}),

without exchanging information across positions or batch elements. Causal self-attention is a sequence mixer. After projecting hidden states to queries, keys, and values,

Q,K,V∈ℝB×S×dh,Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times d_{h}},

the output at position tt in batch element bb is a weighted sum of value vectors from earlier positions in the same sequence,

Attn(X)b,t,:=∑s≤tαb,t,sVb,s,:.\operatorname{Attn}(X)_{b,t,:}=\sum_{s\leq t}\alpha_{b,t,s}V_{b,s,:}.

Thus ordinary causal attention mixes over the sequence index ss, but keeps the batch index fixed.

Batch-mixing changes the attention mask so that tokens can also read from other batch elements. In practice, batch-mixing architectures cannot allow all tokens to communicate across the batch, as this quickly becomes computationally intractable.

3.3 BatchParScale

ParScale creates multiple prefix-conditioned streams, but those streams are independent until the final aggregation.

We now introduce BatchParScale (BPS), our first batch-mixing architecture in which BB parallel streams are grouped in one forward pass and only designated communication positions may attend across streams.

A small set of communication positions mediates information flow between otherwise independent streams. Each stream is processed as its own causal sequence through the shared Transformer, so cross-stream reads are a restricted form of cross-attention where queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another.

For each original sequence, we create PP streams and group them as a single communication set. Let Hp(ℓ)∈ℝn×dH^{(\ell)}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} denote the hidden states of stream pp entering layer ℓ\ell. As in the traditional Transformer, each stream produces

Qp(ℓ),Kp,x(ℓ),Vp,x(ℓ)∈ℝn×dh.Q^{(\ell)}_{p},\quad K^{(\ell)}_{p,x},\quad V^{(\ell)}_{p,x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}}.

Rather than prepend stream-specific prefix caches, we designate a sparse set of virtual tokens Cp(ℓ)⊆{1,…,n}C^{(\ell)}_{p}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} for stream pp at layer ℓ\ell.

Let K(ℓ)K^{(\ell)} and V(ℓ)V^{(\ell)} stack the keys and values of all PP streams,

K(ℓ)\displaystyle K^{(\ell)} =[K1,x(ℓ);…;KP,x(ℓ)],\displaystyle=\left[K^{(\ell)}_{1,x};\ldots;K^{(\ell)}_{P,x}\right],
V(ℓ)\displaystyle V^{(\ell)} =[V1,x(ℓ);…;VP,x(ℓ)]∈ℝP​n×dh,\displaystyle=\left[V^{(\ell)}_{1,x};\ldots;V^{(\ell)}_{P,x}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{Pn\times d_{h}},

so a query in stream pp could in principle attend to any position in any stream. Cross-stream attention is then computed as

Attn⁡(Qp(ℓ),K(ℓ),V(ℓ),M(ℓ)),\operatorname{Attn}\left(Q^{(\ell)}_{p},\,K^{(\ell)},\,V^{(\ell)};M^{(\ell)}\right),

where the mask M(ℓ)M^{(\ell)} restricts attention to the allowed pattern. The mask M(ℓ)M^{(\ell)} preserves ordinary causal attention within each stream. Across streams, it allows attention only between virtual tokens. For a query at stream pp, position tt, and a key-value at stream rr, position ss, attention is allowed exactly when

(p=r∧s≤t)∨(p≠r∧t∈Cp(ℓ)CLOSE\displaystyle\left(p=r\;\land\;s\leq t\right)\;\lor\;\left(p\neq r\;\land\;t\in C^{(\ell)}_{p}\right.
OPEN∧s∈Cr(ℓ)∧s≤t)\displaystyle\left.\;\land\;s\in C^{(\ell)}_{r}\;\land\;s\leq t\right)

Thus non-communication tokens cannot directly read another stream. Cross-stream information must be written into a communication position and then propagated forward through ordinary causal attention.

We experimented with three ways to define Cp(ℓ)C^{(\ell)}_{p}. One approach inserts KK learned vocabulary tokens ([CROSS_ATTEND]) at uniform spacing through the sequence. These tokens have no loss and act only as buffers or scratchpads for moving information from one sequence to another. Another approach keeps sequence length fixed and pre-selects KK ordinary token positions, spread uniformly, as communication positions via the mask. Here the virtual role is assigned to content-bearing hidden states rather than separate buffer tokens, much as Longformer designates selected positions as global attention sites (Beltagy et al., 2020).

Our third approach also routes over existing positions, but learns which positions to expose with a per-layer router in the style of Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024). At each layer, a gate head scores every position,

gp,t(ℓ)=uℓ​(Hp,t(ℓ)),πp,t(ℓ)=σ⁡(gp,t(ℓ)),g^{(\ell)}_{p,t}=u_{\ell}\!\left(H^{(\ell)}_{p,t}\right),\qquad\pi^{(\ell)}_{p,t}=\sigma\!\left(g^{(\ell)}_{p,t}\right),

where σ\sigma is the logistic function and πp,t(ℓ)\pi^{(\ell)}_{p,t} is a per-position Bernoulli parameter. During training and prefill, we do not sample from this distribution. Instead, we select a fixed budget of KK positions per stream by top-KK on the gate logits,

Cp(ℓ)=TopKt⁡(gp,t(ℓ),K),C^{(\ell)}_{p}=\operatorname{TopK}_{t}\left(g^{(\ell)}_{p,t},K\right),

which enforces a sparse cross-stream channel while keeping selection deterministic. The sigmoid gate πp,t(ℓ)\pi^{(\ell)}_{p,t} then scales the attention output at selected positions, letting gradients propagate back to the router. Because top-KK routing is undefined at decode time, where only one new position is visible per step, we add an auxiliary BCE head vℓv_{\ell} that predicts membership from Hp,t(ℓ)H^{(\ell)}_{p,t} alone, enabling causal routing without revisiting past positions. Cross-stream queries and keys are restricted to these routed sites via a FlexAttention block mask (PyTorch Labs, 2024; Dong et al., 2024), which compiles to a fused Triton kernel; unless noted otherwise, our main results use this learned router, denoted Dynamic.

4 Toy Tasks

4.1 Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack

Needle-in-a-haystack is a popular benchmark for measuring whether language models can retrieve information from long contexts (Kamradt, 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Hsieh et al., 2024). To isolate cross-stream retrieval, we introduce a synthetic benchmark called Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack (PNIAH). Each training example is a single long sequence partitioned into BB parallel streams. We call the stream that contains the needle the holder. The holder can answer the question using only local retrieval. The remaining streams are non-holders and their answer can only depend on information from other streams.

We report holder accuracy AHA_{H} and non-holder accuracy AN​HA_{NH} separately. Each plotted point uses 1000 evaluation examples, so AHA_{H} is measured over 1000 holder streams and AN​HA_{NH} over 1000​(B−1)1000(B-1) non-holder streams.

We conduct a sweep over sequence lengths from 128,256,…​1024128,256,\dots 1024, batch sizes B=4,8B=4,8 and hidden sizes d=32,64,128d=32,64,128. We use four-layer Transformer models that follow the Qwen3 architecture except for the attention mechanism (Yang et al., 2025). Figure 2 visualizes holder and non-holder accuracies. The xx-axis is haystack length and the yy-axis is accuracy. Rows fix hidden size and columns fix BB.

Most models in this sweep solve the holder task, and larger models often solve the non-holder task as well. Counterintuitively, in some settings, non-holder accuracy increases with sequence length.

5 Pretraining

Having shown in toy experiments that batch-mixing can move information across sequences, we next ask whether cross-stream communication helps ordinary language-model pretraining.

For our experiments, we use TinyStories (Eldan and Li, 2023), which is small enough for controlled architecture comparisons while still requiring coherent next-token prediction.

We compare 3 model families on TinyStories. As a baseline reference we train a standard Qwen3 architecture (Yang et al., 2025). We train ParScale at B=4B=4 and B=8B=8 (Chen et al., 2025) so we can compare directly against BatchParScale under the same multi-stream setup. Our main models are BatchParScale with Static and Dynamic, at B=4B=4 and B=8B=8.

To facilitate the learning of cross-sequence communication, we add noise in the form of masking tokens to each sequence independently, thus forcing sequences to attend to each other to recover lost information. However for a 1-1 comparison to ParScale we also include training runs with masking disabled.

All models are GPT-2-scale with hyperparameters: 12 layers, dmodel=768d_{\mathrm{model}}=768, 12 attention heads, MLP width 3072, and a 50,257-token vocabulary, otherwise using the Qwen3 architecture (Yang et al., 2025).

In addition to next-token cross-entropy, we evaluate whether BatchParScale can move specific information across streams with a benchmark we name Parallel-QA (PQA).

Each example contains a source record, a masked query, and five candidate completions; we place the record and query in different streams. For each candidate ci=(y1,…,yT)c_{i}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}), we score the teacher-forced completion as

si=∑t=1Tlog⁡pθ​(yt∣x,y<t).s_{i}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).

The predicted answer is the highest-scoring candidate. Accuracy (ArgMax) reports whether that candidate is correct, while rank reports the position of the correct candidate after sorting by score. The concatenated variant puts the record and query in a single ordinary sequence, allowing us to test whether standard within-stream attention can solve the candidate-scoring problem. This setup isolates model capability from cross-stream attention, making it possible to distinguish limitations due to the model itself from those arising specifically from cross-stream communication. Appendix F gives a concrete example of the prompt and stream layout.

Table 1 summarizes the final eval losses. The training-loss curves are shown in Appendix B, Figure 7.

We find that the BatchParScale models cluster around eval loss 1.008-1.014, a small 0.009-0.015 nats below ParScale B=4B=4.

The 30%30\% masked variants also remain below the Qwen3 baseline (Yang et al., 2025), meaning that even when a meaningful portion of the sequence is garbled, our model is able to predict the next token better than the baseline, by retrieving the right context from other sequences. For the ParScale baselines, we use the same aggregation label-smoothing parameter as the ParScale paper, ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1 (Chen et al., 2025). Even with this matched regularizer, ParScale B=8B=8 is substantially worse than ParScale B=4B=4, suggesting stream collapse or under-utilization of streams.

The concatenated column separates model capability from cross-stream communication. Static-BPS reaches perfect concatenated accuracy, showing that ordinary attention can solve the probe when the evidence and query are in one sequence. Its lower cross accuracy on the other hand, shows that the model is not yet able to retrieve important facts from other sequences. Dynamic-BPS has the best aggregate losses, but remains weak even in the concatenated condition, so its low cross accuracy should not be interpreted only as a communication failure, and although its loss is slightly better than Static-BPS, it is not able to solve these. We therefore find that aggregate loss improvements do not, by themselves, demonstrate reliable communication of specific facts between streams.

Figure 3 tracks masked-token argmax accuracy during pretraining on the duplicated 30%30\%-masked validation setup. With cross-stream attention enabled, all four models eventually reach roughly 50%50\% argmax accuracy on masked positions. The lower panel isolates the cross-stream contribution by subtracting the same diagnostic with cross-stream attention disabled. Dynamic-BPS shows a clear gain, reaching about 1212–1616 percentage points by the end of training, with the largest benefit at B=8B=8. Static-BPS remains near zero throughout, indicating that its loss improvement in Table 1 is not driven by recovery of masked tokens through the cross-stream channel. These results suggest that dynamic routing learns to borrow cross-stream evidence at corrupted positions, while static routing benefits mainly through generic contextual information rather than recovering specific masked tokens. This hints that alternative data augmentation methods or loss functions might be needed to better incentivize cross-stream communication.

The comparison also shows that dynamic routing is not uniformly better: it improves masked-token recovery, but it does not perform well on PQA.

Figure 4 inspects how the Dynamic-BPS router implements this behavior on 500 non-overlapping TinyStories validation chunks from the B=4B=4, 30%30\% masked model. The router selects 12 positions per stream in every layer. The top panel reports both directions of mask-router coupling: the fraction of virtual tokens that are masks, and the fraction of masked or unmasked tokens that are routed as virtual. Masks are strongly privileged as communication sites (P⁡(virtual∣mask)≈0.31P(\mathrm{virtual}\mid\mathrm{mask})\approx 0.31 at layer 1 versus P⁡(virtual∣unmasked)≈0.003P(\mathrm{virtual}\mid\mathrm{unmasked})\approx 0.003), while layers 1 and 2 also route masks for 98.0%98.0\% and 100.0%100.0\% of virtual positions. The middle panel reports mean cross-stream attention mass from virtual communication positions to virtual keys in other streams, split by whether the query token is masked or unmasked; at layer 1, masked virtual queries route more aggressively than unmasked ones (0.340.34 versus 0.240.24). The bottom panel decomposes each virtual query’s full attention budget into same-stream non-virtual context, same-stream virtual keys, and cross-stream virtual keys.

Together, Figures 3 and 4 show that Dynamic-BPS learns to route cross-stream communication through corrupted local positions, but they do not yet identify whether the information comes from semantically matched neighboring streams.

To obtain visual intuition for this mechanism, we also created an interactive artifact for the Dynamic-BPS B=4B=4, 30%30\% masked model. The viewer is available here; it lets readers inspect token grids, cross-stream attention edges, and ablation heatmaps for the captured examples. Qualitatively, it shows the same pattern as Figure 4: early layers preferentially select masked tokens as communication sites, while at later layers, relay mass frequently flows through structural anchor points instead of directly targeting the exact visible copy of the masked token. Appendix C gives a targeted positional-offset diagnostic for these captures. Across four masked TinyStories attention-flow runs, cross-stream attention often concentrates on the same sequence position in neighboring streams, and relay mass concentrates near the aligned position even when the aligned token in the other stream is also masked. This suggests that the masked-copy setup can induce a positional addressing shortcut rather than fully content-addressed retrieval.

5.1 Is BatchParScale Selective?

The masked TinyStories results show that batch-mixing can improve language-model loss, but they do not identify what kind of cross-stream information is being used. In the standard masked diagnostic, all four streams are drawn from TinyStories, so neighboring streams will always contain useful distributional context. We therefore evaluate a different setting where not all sequences will be informative, and study whether the virtual tokens have learned to be selective in what information they attend to. For this analysis, we use the Dynamic-BPS B=4B=4, 30%30\% masked TinyStories model and compare masked-token loss with cross-stream attention enabled and disabled.

Each evaluation batch contains four streams. We consider three versions. First, all streams are drawn from a single TinyStories validation batch with 30%30\% masking applied, denoted A​A​A​AAAAA or B​B​B​BBBBB. Second, streams are split between two disjoint TinyStories validation sequences, denoted A​A​B​BAABB. Third, half the streams are TinyStories and half are uniformly random token sequences, denoted A​A​U​UAAUU or B​B​U​UBBUU. We found that stream order didn’t matter for results, so we report the source layouts without separate order variants. All results in Table 2 use 100 masked evaluation batches with masking rate 0.30.3 for Dynamic-BPS B=4B=4.

Batch-mixing improves masked CE on real TinyStories streams in every condition. The improvement is similar when all neighboring streams are real TinyStories, when the batch mixes two disjoint TinyStories streams, and when half of the neighboring streams are random tokens. In contrast, the random streams do not benefit. Their loss slightly increases when cross-stream attention is enabled.

We also measure how attention is distributed over sequences. Let SS denote the set of virtual token positions in a batch and let αq,k\alpha_{q,k} be the attention weight from a virtual token qq to key k∈Sk\in S. We renormalize over all virtual tokens,

α~q,k=αq,k∑k′∈Sαq,k′,\tilde{\alpha}_{q,k}=\frac{\alpha_{q,k}}{\sum_{k^{\prime}\in S}\alpha_{q,k^{\prime}}},

and report the mass landing on each sequence separately (Mass R0–R3 in Table 2).

We find that sequences allocate relatively little attention mass to sequences different from the source. For example, in AABB and AAUU all rows for B and U get around 0.125 of the probability mass, despite B being more informative than the random noise in U. Thus we find that the model does exhibit selectivity: it can ignore foreign sequences, but it does not distinguish between sequences that are different but still informative (B) and completely random sequences (U).

Even with noisy neighboring streams, masked CE on AA or BB is lower than the ordinary unmasked next-token CE of the pretrained TinyStories Qwen baseline measured on the same source-mismatch validation setup.

6 Continued Pretraining with LoRA

We next ask whether the same mechanisms can be used when starting from an existing pretrained language model. To study this, we ran a 100M-token FineWeb-Edu continued-pretraining comparison using Qwen3-0.6B with sequence length 512 (Penedo et al., 2024). The multi-stream models use B=4B=4, K=12K=12 virtual tokens, and LoRA rank 64 with alpha 128. Table 3 reports the final LM losses and evaluation scores across PNIAH and PMHQA-style datasets. For all candidate-scoring probes, including WikiHop, we rank candidates by mean token log-probability. Training curves for these runs are shown in Appendix D, Figure 8.

As a stronger task-specific control, we also fine-tune a BatchParScale B=4B=4 adapter directly on WikiHop with split evidence across parallel streams (Appendix H). Each example forms one batch-parallel forward pass: three support documents occupy separate streams and a fourth target stream contains the query and supervised answer tokens, with LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B and dynamic cross-stream attention enabled. Training minimizes the split-evidence objective

ℒsplit=−∑i∈𝒜tlogpθ(yt,i∣x1:B,yt,<i),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{split}}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{t,i}\mid x_{1:B},y_{t,<i}\right),

so only target answer tokens are supervised while evidence streams still influence predictions through cross-stream attention.

The LM-loss result is encouraging for ordinary continued pretraining: ParScale and the no-mask BatchParScale run both improve over the Qwen3 LoRA baseline. For the masked LoRA runs, we also log the same masked-context diagnostic used in TinyStories pretraining: masked-token argmax accuracy with cross-stream attention enabled versus disabled on duplicated validation batches. Appendix Figure 9 shows a clear gap, reaching roughly 1414 percentage points on the 30%30\%-mask run and 1010 percentage points on the 50%50\%-mask run, suggesting that the fine-tuned model uses neighboring streams to recover corrupted tokens.

The QA diagnostics in Table 3 show a sharper limitation. The plain Qwen baselines solve the concatenated versions of PNIAH and PMHQA, so the tasks are answerable when all evidence is placed in one ordinary context. The BatchParScale adapters, however, remain close to chance on non-holder PNIAH and PMHQA, and disabling cross-stream attention is often comparable or better.

WikiHop, however, shows a different pattern: the concatenated baseline reaches 36% accuracy, whereas our CPT adapters reach 20–27%, meaningfully above chance and close to the dedicated BatchParScale B=4B=4 WikiHop fine-tuning run at 30%.

For additional notes on QA-finetuning experiments and methods see Appendix H.

7 Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Our longer-term motivation is not only to let parallel streams exchange information, but to let them learn coordinated strategies. This section studies multi-agent coordination problems at a small scale. Each agent’s observation history is treated as a stream, and the policy must learn when information from other streams is useful for coordinated action.

We study six policy classes: MLP, RNN, Temporal Transformer, Agent Transformer, Temporal-Agent Transformer, and BatchParScale. For each environment state, agent ii at time tt observes ot,io_{t,i}, which is embedded into a token ht,ih_{t,i}. The policy outputs an action distribution

πθ(at,i∣⋅)=Softmax(Wπzt,i),\pi_{\theta}(a_{t,i}\mid\cdot)=\operatorname{Softmax}(W_{\pi}z_{t,i}),

where zt,iz_{t,i} is the final representation for that agent and timestep. In our current implementations, transformer tokens are observation-history tokens, not separate observation and action tokens. Previous actions are used by PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) for the policy-gradient objective, and available-action masks are applied to the output logits, but actions are not fed back as tokens in the attention sequence. The Temporal Transformer applies causal attention independently within each agent’s history,

(t,i)←(s,i),s≤t.(t,i)\leftarrow(s,i),\quad s\leq t.

The Agent Transformer attends across agents only at the current timestep,

(t,i)←(t,j).(t,i)\leftarrow(t,j).

The Temporal-Agent Transformer flattens time and agents into one sequence and allows dense causal attention across both axes,

(t,i)←(s,j),s≤t.(t,i)\leftarrow(s,j),\quad s\leq t.

At long sequences, this architecture becomes infeasible. It is also a natural upper reference for BatchParScale, because it can use dense attention across agents and time rather than communicating only through selected positions.

BatchParScale keeps a separate temporal stream for each agent and permits cross-agent communication only through selected virtual tokens,

(t,i)←(s,j)only ifi≠j,(t,i)\leftarrow(s,j)\quad\text{only if}\quad i\neq j,
t∈Ci,s∈Cj,s≤t.t\in C_{i},\quad s\in C_{j},\quad s\leq t.

We note that BatchParScale is at a significant disadvantage compared to our most expressive model Temporal-Agent-Transformer which can do full dense attention across all streams.

All policies are trained with a MAPPO-style actor-critic objective. This follows the centralized-training, decentralized-execution paradigm: the critic receives centralized world-state histories during training, while the actor acts from per-agent observation histories. For BatchParScale, Agent-Transformer, and Temporal-Agent-Transformer, decentralized execution still includes learned communication, because each agent stream can read selected hidden states from other agent streams. For each policy class, the critic receives centralized world-state histories and uses the corresponding architecture family. The comparison therefore keeps the MAPPO-style training setup fixed across policies, but it does not hold the critic architecture fixed.

7.1 MPE

The MPE tasks are small but communication-sensitive coordination problems (Lowe et al., 2017). Table 4 reports the three-seed results. On Simple Spread and Simple Reference, BatchParScale is competitive with the Temporal-Agent Transformer.

7.2 SMAX

SMAX is a harder stress test for sparse virtual-token communication, implemented through the JaxMARL SMAX suite (Samvelyan et al., 2019; Rutherford et al., 2023). Table 5 summarizes the main SMAX comparison. Across three rerun seeds, the strongest policies vary substantially, while the temporal-attention policies fail on this task with consistently low scores. BatchParScale remains close to the temporal and Temporal-Agent transformer means, but all agent communication mechanisms are weak on this task and a simple MLP performs best, suggesting multi-agent coordination is not critical for this task.

7.3 MABrax

MABrax gives a continuous-control counterexample to the MPE gains (Freeman et al., 2021; Rutherford et al., 2023). Table 6 reports the HalfCheetah results. BatchParScale learns and improves over the MLP baseline, but it underperforms the temporal and agent transformers on this HalfCheetah task.

7.4 Jumanji Search and Rescue

SearchAndRescue tests partial observability more directly (Bonnet et al., 2024). Table 7 reports the main SearchAndRescue setting. For results varying the number of vision rays and searchers, see Figure 10.

Appendix Table 8 reports a sweep over the visibility parameter. BatchParScale beats Temporal-Agent in four of six settings.

Overall, BatchParScale participates in learned coordination: strong on MPE, competitive on SearchAndRescue. They are also mixed: BatchParScale underperforms on MABrax and does not solve the harder SMAX setting. Sparse communication is therefore useful, but not a complete substitute for denser temporal-agent attention.

8 Performance and Hardware-Aware Cross-Stream Attention Mechanisms

The computational appeal of B​a​t​c​h​P​a​r​S​c​a​l​eBatchParScale{} is that streams or sequences communicate through a small set of tokens rather than through fully dense attention. With BB streams of length nn, independent causal attention costs O⁡(B​n2)O(Bn^{2}), while allowing every token in every stream to attend across all streams costs O⁡(B2​n2)O(B^{2}n^{2}). If each stream exposes only K=nvirtualK=n_{\mathrm{virtual}} communication positions, the intended cost becomes O⁡(B​n2+B2​K2)O(Bn^{2}+B^{2}K^{2}). However, Figure 5 shows that the asymptotic advantage does not show up in practice, and BatchParScale has a large overhead and even runs slower than fully dense cross-stream attention.

The direct implementation is slow because FlexAttention does not handle the resulting irregular mask efficiently.

We thus propose a two-pass implementation. Let SpS_{p} be the selected positions in stream pp, and let Hp∈ℝn×dH_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be its hidden states. The first pass runs local causal attention within each stream. The second pass gathers the selected states into a compact block:

Z\displaystyle Z =Gather⁡({Hp​[Sp]}p=1B),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Gather}\left(\{H_{p}[S_{p}]\}_{p=1}^{B}\right),
Z\displaystyle Z ∈ℝB​K×d.\displaystyle\in\mathbb{R}^{BK\times d}.

For a selected query ii, let AiA_{i} be its local-causal key set and let GiG_{i} be the gathered selected-key set with keys already present in AiA_{i} removed. The two attention passes produce local and global outputs yiAy_{i}^{A} and yiGy_{i}^{G}, while retaining their log normalizers:

siA\displaystyle s_{i}^{A} =log∑j∈Aiexp(qi⊤kj/d),\displaystyle=\log\sum_{j\in A_{i}}\exp(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}),
siG\displaystyle s_{i}^{G} =log∑j∈Giexp(qi⊤kj/d).\displaystyle=\log\sum_{j\in G_{i}}\exp(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}).

The virtual token output is then merged as

yi2​p​a​s​s=exp⁡(siA)​yiA+exp⁡(siG)​yiGexp⁡(siA)+exp⁡(siG).y_{i}^{\mathrm{2pass}}=\frac{\exp(s_{i}^{A})y_{i}^{A}+\exp(s_{i}^{G})y_{i}^{G}}{\exp(s_{i}^{A})+\exp(s_{i}^{G})}.

Because AiA_{i} and GiG_{i} are disjoint, this is exactly the same softmax as attention over Ai∪GiA_{i}\cup G_{i}, which is the original selected-token mask. The merge is the standard log-sum-exp combination used in FlashAttention-style tiled kernels. The cost is O⁡(B​n2)+O⁡((B​K)2)O(Bn^{2})+O((BK)^{2}), and the O⁡((B​K)2)O((BK)^{2}) term is computed by its own small dense attention kernel.

Another benefit of this decomposition is that, as in Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), we can use separate query, key, and value projections for the local causal pass and for attention over gathered virtual-token states, without changing the merged output above. Dedicated projections would let virtual-token queries and keys specialize for cross-stream retrieval rather than reusing representations tuned for local language modeling.

Figure 6 compares our two-pass implementation with local causal attention and dense attention across sequences. Two-pass BatchParScale remains close to the local causal baseline, while fully dense attention becomes increasingly expensive as sequence length and batch count grow.

9 Conclusion

In this paper we introduce batch-mixing as a new class of sequence models for coordinated parallel computation. For a concrete and hardware-efficient instantiation of such a model we proposed BatchParScale, and showed that, when implemented carefully, it can exhibit negligible overhead compared to standard self-attention. We showed it can learn controlled cross-stream retrieval on parallel-needle-in-a-haystack, outperforms ParScale on language modelling on TinyStories and FineWeb-Edu, and can perform competitively on many MARL tasks.

Although 30%-masked BatchParScale models beat the Qwen baseline on pretraining loss and cross-stream attention improves masked-token recovery, we find that on PNIAH all models meaningfully underperform the concatenated version, suggesting that streams still cannot reliably recover facts from parallel streams. PMHQA remains near chance despite strong holder accuracy, suggesting that language-modelling loss improvements do not yet correlate with reliable retrieval to streams that must answer without local evidence. This suggests that our current pretraining approach alone does not incentivize the cross-stream retrieval and communication these benchmarks measure. Also, whereas BatchParScale at 30% noise was able to outperform the baseline on pretraining, we do not find this to be the case for finetuning. Whether this is due to the much harder language-modelling objective or the smaller space of weights to tune remains in question.

Future work should focus on better training objectives and data augmentation techniques to incentivize multi-sequence communication and coordination. For example, instead of just masking, we could mix in or rephrase data from other streams to encourage true cross-sequence reasoning instead of copying. Additionally, future experiments should further extend pretraining and finetuning to larger model sizes, helping us understand how this method performs at larger scales and on more challenging data mixtures.

Appendix C Positional Copy-Shortcut Diagnostics

The masked TinyStories experiments duplicate a validation sequence across parallel streams and independently mask each stream. This setup is useful because a masked token in one stream may be visible in another stream. However, exact duplication also creates a possible shortcut: the model can address the same sequence position in another stream rather than retrieve by content. We therefore run a positional-offset diagnostic on four Dynamic-BPS attention-flow captures with B∈{4,8}B\in\{4,8\}, masking rates 30%30\% and 50%50\%, and sequence length 128.

For every cross-stream attention edge from query position tt to key position ss, we record the relative offset

Δ=s−t.\Delta=s-t.

We aggregate attention mass over Δ\Delta per layer and per head. A concentration at Δ=0\Delta=0 means that a head reads the aligned position in another stream. For masked queries, we additionally inspect relay sources from the attention-flow artifact. The relay score composes head-mean local attention before and after one cross-stream bridge, then records the largest source positions contributing to each masked query. This gives a coarse source-level view of where cross-stream information appears to originate.

The diagnostic shows two related effects. First, some heads are strongly position locked. In the B=8B=8 runs, late-layer heads such as L9H4, L9H7, and L9H9 put roughly 85%85\%–94%94\% of their cross-stream attention mass on Δ=0\Delta=0. These heads mostly read the same position in another stream. Second, the relay-source diagnostic shows that exactly aligned relay mass is often larger for non-oracle aligned positions than for oracle aligned positions. That is, relay mass can land on the same position in a neighboring stream even when that position is also masked.

The relay mass is not only concentrated at the exact aligned token. Around 37%37\%–42%42\% of top-source relay mass lies within four tokens of the aligned position, far above the uniform baseline of about 3.5%3.5\% for a length-128 sequence. The largest offsets are typically just before the query position. This suggests a mechanism in which the model imports local context from the aligned neighborhood of another stream, rather than directly copying the visible target token itself.

These results support a positional-addressing interpretation of the masked-copy gains. Cross-stream attention appears to exploit the fact that the streams are exact aligned copies, so the same position or nearby positions in another stream are likely to contain useful context. This is useful for masked-token recovery, but it is weaker than content-addressed retrieval. It also helps explain why aggregate masked-token improvements do not necessarily translate into reliable transfer of non-redundant facts in PNIAH, PMHQA, or WikiHop-style probes.

This diagnostic has important limitations. It uses attention weights rather than value norms or direct logit attribution, and the relay source analysis is truncated to the top recorded sources per masked query. The relay computation also uses head-mean attention and a restricted local-to-cross-to-local path form. A stronger causal test would shift the duplicated streams by kk tokens and measure masked-token recovery as a function of kk, or inject disagreeing copies and test whether predictions follow the copied stream against local context.

Appendix H Parallel-MHQA Fine-Tuning

This appendix gives the details behind the QA diagnostics summarized in Table 3. We use these probes to test whether the masked-context benefit in continued pretraining corresponds to usable cross-stream transfer.

Parallel-NIAH (PNIAH) extends the holder/non-holder setup from Section 4.1 to real FineWeb-Edu documents. Each example has B=4B=4 parallel streams, one randomly chosen holder stream contains a synthetic needle of the form The secret access code is ‘‘XXX-YYYY’’, and the remaining non-holder streams contain unrelated text with the answer redacted. At evaluation time, every stream is asked for the code and scored with a 10-way multiple-choice test over synthetic codes in the same format: the true answer plus nine randomly generated distractors. For each candidate we teacher-force the completion and rank options by mean token log-probability, following the same candidate-scoring procedure as ParallelQA; chance is 0.10.1. We report non-holder accuracy AN​HA_{NH}, i.e. whether streams that do not locally contain the needle select the correct code. Holder accuracy measures only local retrieval and is therefore not the metric of interest here. This design avoids treating target-row shortcuts or memorized NIAH benchmark facts as evidence of cross-stream communication.

Parallel-MHQA (PMHQA) extends ParallelQA to a split-evidence multi-hop setting. ParallelQA in Section 5 tests single-hop cross-stream retrieval: a source record in one stream must help a masked query in another select among five name completions. PMHQA is not built from an existing multi-hop benchmark; we generate 100 fully synthetic two-hop cases with random person names, project titles, and reference codes. Each case is authored as two short records that form a controlled chain; for example, “Record 1: Aria assigned reference code ABC-123 to the Cedar initiative” and “Record 2: Milo says Nora should use Aria’s reference for the Cedar initiative”. We place the two records on separate streams while a target stream asks which code Nora should use. The target stream lists four synthetic code options and is scored with the same teacher-forced candidate-ranking procedure as ParallelQA; chance and the best constant-position baseline are both 0.250.25. Answering therefore depends on chaining both facts through cross-stream attention, not on retrieving a single locally absent fact or on pretrained WikiHop-style knowledge. We run this probe on continued-pretraining adapters rather than the TinyStories from-scratch models, because the multi-hop composition is substantially harder and would be difficult to interpret on models whose reasoning capacity is still largely untrained.

Both communication diagnostics remain weak. On PNIAH, AN​HA_{NH} remains close to chance even though holder accuracy is near perfect. The multi-hop QA probe is also near chance: the BatchParScale runs reach 0.260.26, 0.220.22, and 0.300.30, and the controls with cross-stream attention disabled are 0.350.35, 0.340.34, and 0.290.29, respectively. On two of the three settings, disabling the cross-stream channel is better, so the channel can actively hurt this probe or the differences are noise at n=100n=100. For this task we also trained a non-holder-only objective,

ℒnonholder=−∑b≠h∑i∈𝒜blogpθ(yb,i∣x1:B,yb,<i),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nonholder}}=-\sum_{b\neq h}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{b}}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{b,i}\mid x_{1:B},y_{b,<i}\right),

where hh is the holder stream. Fine-tuning an existing LM can preserve or mobilize local knowledge and can lower language-model loss, but reliable transfer to streams that do not contain the evidence remains unresolved. Reliable transfer to non-holder streams is the clearest failure we observe, and it makes routing the natural target for future work.

We also run direct split-evidence QA fine-tuning probes. The goal is to test a stronger intervention than continued pretraining: if we explicitly fine-tune the model on answer supervision where evidence is placed in neighboring streams, does it learn to retrieve those facts through batch-mixing? Table 13 summarizes these direct fine-tuning controls. These experiments are useful mainly as controls, because standard QA datasets can be answered from target-row artifacts or pretrained knowledge. Each example is represented as BB streams. Some streams contain evidence, while one target stream contains the question and answer format. Unless otherwise stated, only answer tokens on the target stream contribute to the supervised loss:

ℒsplit=−∑i∈𝒜tlogpθ(yt,i∣x1:B,yt,<i),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{split}}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{t,i}\mid x_{1:B},y_{t,<i}\right),

where 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is the set of answer-token positions in target stream tt. The evidence streams still participate in the forward pass and can influence the target prediction through cross-stream attention, but they are not asked to reproduce the target answer. For the matched isolated control we disable batch-mixing and train the same target loss,

ℒisolated=−∑i∈𝒜tlogpθ(yt,i∣xt,yt,<i).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{isolated}}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{t,i}\mid x_{t},y_{t,<i}\right).

A high isolated-control result means that the benchmark is not cleanly measuring cross-stream evidence. It suggests that pretrained knowledge, benchmark artifacts, or target-row shortcuts can explain the apparent gain.

We ran these probes on WikiHop-style candidate scoring (Welbl et al., 2018), QASC (Khot et al., 2020), and two guarded synthetic multiple-choice tasks. WikiHop reaches 0.300 in the best direct split-evidence run, but the isolated split control already reaches 0.230, far above the random-candidate baseline. QASC is even less clean: a base model with only the question and answer options reaches 0.454, close to the best split cross-stream result of 0.472. These results show that pretrained knowledge, candidate-list artifacts, and target-row lexical signal can explain much of the apparent success.

The guarded synthetic tasks remove those shortcuts and give a sharper negative result. On the first guarded synthetic task, the isolated control remains at chance, but the best cross-stream run is only 0.146 and the correct-answer probability remains essentially uniform. Synthetic QA-v4 makes the same point more directly: a full-context SFT model reaches 0.984 accuracy when both evidence rows are placed in one sequence, while the isolated split model reaches 0.117 and the best split cross-stream variant reaches only 0.164. We also tried reader variants that scored candidates stream-by-stream, message variants that placed short summaries in communication positions, and latent-memory variants with extra shared slots, but none closed the gap to full context. By this standard, the current multi-hop QA results are short probes rather than final benchmarks.

Appendix J Default Cross-Stream Attention Mask

We define the mask used for the default sparse cross-stream attention pattern, omitting implementation switches for dropout, padding, and ablation modes. Consider one original example expanded into BB streams. Within a layer ℓ\ell, index a query by (p,t)(p,t) and a key-value by (r,s)(r,s), where p,r∈{1,…,B}p,r\in\{1,\ldots,B\} are stream indices and t,s∈{1,…,n}t,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\} are sequence positions. Let Cp(ℓ)⊆{1,…,n}C^{(\ell)}_{p}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} be the communication positions selected for stream pp. The Boolean allow-mask is defined by

A(p,t),(r,s)(ℓ)=1A^{(\ell)}_{(p,t),(r,s)}=1

if and only if either

p=rands≤t,p=r\quad\text{and}\quad s\leq t,

or

p≠r,t∈Cp(ℓ),s∈Cr(ℓ),s≤t.p\neq r,\quad t\in C^{(\ell)}_{p},\quad s\in C^{(\ell)}_{r},\quad s\leq t.

Equivalently, same-stream tokens use standard causal self-attention, while cross-stream attention is available only from a communication query position to a communication key-value position in another stream, with the same causal order constraint. The additive attention mask used in the softmax is

M(p,t),(r,s)(ℓ)={0,A(p,t),(r,s)(ℓ)=1,−∞,A(p,t),(r,s)(ℓ)=0.M^{(\ell)}_{(p,t),(r,s)}=\begin{cases}0,&A^{(\ell)}_{(p,t),(r,s)}=1,\\ -\infty,&A^{(\ell)}_{(p,t),(r,s)}=0.\end{cases}

For a static virtual-token model, Cp(ℓ)C^{(\ell)}_{p} is the fixed set of virtual-token positions. For a routed model, Cp(ℓ)C^{(\ell)}_{p} is the layerwise top-KK set selected by the router.

J.1 FlexAttention Mask Implementation

In FlexAttention, the mask is implemented as a Boolean mask_mod rather than as a materialized additive mask (PyTorch Labs, 2024; Dong et al., 2024). We flatten the stream and sequence axes inside each communication group:

flat⁡(p,t)=p⋅n+t.\mathrm{flat}(p,t)=p\cdot n+t.

Thus FlexAttention calls mask_mod with flattened query and key-value indices. The default sparse rule is implemented by recovering the stream and position indices, then returning the local causal rule or the cross-stream communication rule:

def mask_mod(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
    q_stream = q_idx // seq_len
    q_pos = q_idx % seq_len
    kv_stream = kv_idx // seq_len
    kv_pos = kv_idx % seq_len

    same_stream = (
        q_stream == kv_stream
    )
    causal = kv_pos <= q_pos
    local = same_stream & causal

    q_selected = selected[
        b, q_stream, q_pos
    ]
    kv_selected = selected[
        b, kv_stream, kv_pos
    ]
    cross = (
        (~same_stream)
        & q_selected
        & kv_selected
        & causal
    )

    return local | cross

Here selected has shape (G,P,n)(G,P,n), where GG is the number of original examples in the batch after grouping, PP is the number of streams, and nn is the per-stream sequence length. The tensors passed to FlexAttention have shape (G,H,P​n,dh)(G,H,Pn,d_{h}), obtained by reshaping from (G,P,H,n,dh)(G,P,H,n,d_{h}). The full call is:

q_flat = q.permute(
    0, 2, 1, 3, 4
).reshape(G, H, P * n, d_h)
k_flat = k.permute(
    0, 2, 1, 3, 4
).reshape(G, H, P * n, d_h)
v_flat = v.permute(
    0, 2, 1, 3, 4
).reshape(G, H, P * n, d_h)

block_mask = create_block_mask(
    mask_mod,
    B=G,
    H=H,
    Q_LEN=P * n,
    KV_LEN=P * n,
    device=q.device,
)

out_flat = flex_attention(
    q_flat,
    k_flat,
    v_flat,
    block_mask=block_mask,
)

out = out_flat.reshape(
    G, H, P, n, d_h
).permute(0, 2, 1, 3, 4)

For static virtual tokens, selected is a fixed Boolean position mask broadcast across groups and streams. For dynamic routing, selected is produced by a per-stream top-KK router over sequence positions.
